title: Impact of Ski Piste Management on Soil Microbial Activity in the Southern Alps, Italy
content: Ski piste development and management provide recreational and economic benefits in mountain regions. However, piste development and management often introduce anthropogenic disturbances: slope grading, technical snowmaking, and infrastructure installation may alter soil properties, vegetation structure, and microclimatic conditions, raising concerns about potential impacts on soil biochemical functioning. This study evaluated the impact of ski-piste management on soil microbial activity across one medium‑sized (MS) and three small‑sized (SS) ski resorts. Paired piste (P)-control (C) plots were established, and sampling was conducted over two consecutive summers in MS and for one year in SS ski resorts. Comparisons between P and adjacent C soils showed no statistically significant differences (p > 0.05) in enzymatic activity or microbial biomass in both ski resorts. In contrast, interannual variation was associated with significant differences in microbial biomass and most enzyme activities (p < 0.05). Piste soils consistently exhibited higher pH than control soils, although this shift did not correspond to detectable changes in biochemical functioning. Overall, ski piste management did not significantly affect soil biochemical functioning under the conditions investigated, whereas interannual variability appeared to be more strongly driven by differences in soil moisture and snow cover. Continued monitoring at broader spatial and temporal scales is essential to assess the long‑term ecological consequences of ski resorts in mountain grasslands.
